title: Cache priming latency sketch and microbench log
content:
Goal:
- Quick personal log for experiments on cache-priming strategies and their effect on tail latency during bursty arrivals. Want concise numbers and actionable follow-ups, not polished writeup.

Context / motivation:
- Production has recurrent short bursts (2–8s) with high fraction of unique prefixes (customer chat sessions). Cold KV-cache penalties dominate p99 in those windows.
- Hypothesis: cheap priming (prefetching top-k KV entries for a tenant or prefix cluster) reduces p95/p99 during bursts while incurring small token overhead.

Testbed:
- Cluster: 4x A30 nodes in devpool (single-model serving, 16 batch slots each), same as earlier microbench runs but isolated to one shard.
- Model: open-llama-13b-quant (quantized, same runtime profile as canary).
- Workload generator: replay of 10k recent session starts (real traces anonymized), arrival shaped into Poisson bursts with peak qps=220, baseline qps=12.
- Measurement windows: 30s warmup, 180s steady burst, 60s cool-down. Each experiment repeated 3x; numbers below are median across runs.

Experiment matrix:
- BASE: no priming, normal KV cache.
- TOPK-PRIME-10: synchronous priming of top-10 frequently used prefix keys for the tenant before burst.
- ADAPT-PREFETCH: lightweight async prefetch triggered when queue length > 100; prefetch top-20 per active route with backoff.
- STAGGERED-SHOT: staggered priming across nodes (1/4 nodes prime different prefix buckets to spread overhead).

Config notes:
- Priming implemented as GETs for KV shards (simulated), each GET counts as small token op (0.002 token-equivalent cost) to attribute overhead.
- Prefetch parallelism limited to 8 concurrent requests to avoid saturating NIC.

Results (median across 3 runs) — key slice: first 20s of burst (where warm/cold differences matter)
- BASE:
  - observed QPS (burst peak): 215
  - cache hit rate (prefix-level): 12%
  - p50: 28 ms, p95: 410 ms, p99: 1,120 ms
  - tail incidents (latency>800ms): 19 per 180s window

- TOPK-PRIME-10:
  - observed QPS: 212
  - cache hit rate: 58% (improvement concentrated on top prefixes)
  - p50: 30 ms, p95: 120 ms, p99: 280 ms
  - tail incidents: 3 per 180s window
  - notes: priming overhead ~6k small GET ops at start (~0.5s burst of extra control traffic), cost-equivalent negligible compared to reduced token egress.

- ADAPT-PREFETCH:
  - observed QPS: 218
  - cache hit rate: 43% overall (higher during sustained bursts)
  - p50: 29 ms, p95: 160 ms, p99: 420 ms
  - tail incidents: 7 per 180s window
  - notes: better than BASE but worse than TOPK for very short bursts. Good tradeoff when priming for many tenants concurrently.

- STAGGERED-SHOT:
  - observed QPS: 214
  - cache hit rate: 49% aggregated (per-node variance high)
  - p50: 32 ms, p95: 140 ms, p99: 360 ms
  - tail incidents: 5 per 180s window
  - notes: reduces priming spikes on any single node but some sessions routed to node that wasn't primed -> variance in customer experience.

Quick interpretation:
- Simple top-k synchronous priming (TOPK-PRIME-10) produced the biggest single-run reduction in p95/p99 for short bursts. The overhead is a one-time control traffic blip that our infra can absorb.
- Adaptive prefetching is more conservative and scales across many tenants with lower priming cost, but it doesn't fully eliminate worst-case cold-hit tail latency for very short, unpredictable spikes.
- Staggered priming helps avoid node-level saturation but introduces routing-dependent variance; coupled with smart routing (send high-risk sessions to primed nodes) it could be powerful.

Risks / caveats:
- Our test used single-model shard and anonymized prefixes; real tenant diversity may have a fatter tail of unique prefixes, reducing efficacy of top-k priming.
- Priming increases cross-node control plane traffic; need to monitor network queues and NIC CPU during rollout.
- Consistency: primed KV may be stale for customers using latest context writes; priming must respect write-forwarding/lease semantics.

Next experiments (prio):
1) Per-tenant adaptive top-k: combine TOPK with ADAPT to only prime tenants with >X sessions in last Y minutes. Aim: reduce priming ops while preserving p99 improvements.
2) Routing-aware priming: prototype routing table that biases new sessions towards primed nodes for 30s. Measure reduction in per-tenant variance.
3) Cost model: run longer 1-hour runs to quantify token-level cost overhead vs token savings from fewer re-runs / retries at client side.
4) Staleness tests: inject small write events around primed keys and measure correctness and rollback mechanisms.

Quick TODOs (for me):
- Convert TOPK code from local patch to feature-flagged PR (link above) and add metrics for priming GET latencies and NIC utilization. (Riley)
- Add tenant-selection criteria to ADAPT module (Aria to prototype)
- Add routing experiment harness to the replay tool (Diego)

Notes to self (random):
- Consider heuristic: if tenant p95 > 600ms in last 10m and recent session-start-rate > 2/s, auto-prime top-5 prefixes.
- Might be worth trying an LRU-ish sampler to find "fast-growing" prefixes rather than pure frequency for top-k.

Raw logs + plots (attachments):
- I saved raw csvs in /tmp/prime-exp-2025-11-08/ on my laptop; will upload if we want plots.
- Sketch of expected waveform: latency spike down within 2s after priming completes, sustained p95 improvement for ~20–45s depending on burst shape.

End of scratchpad.
